title: Copilot for RFPs: How to Use Microsoft Copilot for RFP Responses
summary: Learn how to use Microsoft Copilot for RFP responses with reusable skills, step-by-step workflows, source verification, and practical prompts to improve accuracy.
body_markdown:
If your team already lives in Microsoft 365, you've probably asked Copilot to help with an RFP at some point. Paste in a question, get back a decent first draft. It works... until you need it to work the same way twice.


That's the real problem with using a general chat assistant for proposals. Every conversation starts from zero. One person asks for a compliance matrix and gets a tidy table with page references. Someone else asks the same thing and gets a loose bullet list with no sources. Nobody remembers the exact prompt that worked last quarter. And nobody can tell which claims came from your approved content and which ones Copilot simply made sound right.


[Microsoft 365 Copilot's Agent Builder](https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365-copilot/build-your-own-agent-with-microsoft-365-copilot) fixes a big chunk of that. You can set up a dedicated RFP agent once, give it clear rules about evidence and traceability, and package your repeatable checks as **custom skills** it uses every time.


We built one ourselves in a Microsoft 365 Copilot work account. This guide walks through exactly what we did, with real screenshots, the prompts we used, and the five skill files we wrote. By the end, you'll have:


- An **RFP Compliance Analyst** agent with sensible guardrails
- An approved SharePoint knowledge base the agent can trust
- Five reusable skills: requirement extraction, source verification, compliance coverage, content freshness, and response consistency
- Copy-ready prompts for every stage of a bid, from go/no-go to final review
- A simple way to measure accuracy before you rely on the agent for a live submission


If you've read our guides on[ChatGPT for RFPs](https://www.inventive.ai/blog-posts/chatgpt-for-rfps) and[Claude for RFPs](https://www.inventive.ai/blog-posts/claude-for-rfps) , this is the Microsoft version of the same idea, adapted to how Copilot actually works.


## **Should you use Microsoft Copilot for RFPs?**


Short answer: if you already pay for Microsoft 365 Copilot and your content lives in SharePoint, it's worth setting up. It won't replace a proposal process, but it can take a lot of grunt work off your plate.


**It's a good fit if:**


- Your team works in Word, Teams, and SharePoint every day
- You handle a handful of RFPs or security questionnaires a month
- You already have reasonably organized, approved content to draw from
- You want a low-cost way to standardize how your team analyzes RFPs


**It's probably not enough on its own if:**


- You respond to high volumes of RFPs with many SMEs involved
- You need assignment tracking, approvals, and audit trails across every bid
- Your answer library is scattered, outdated, or full of conflicting versions
- You routinely export answers into buyer portals or complex spreadsheets


### **Which Copilot do you need?**


Microsoft uses the Copilot name for several different products, which makes this confusing. Here's the short version for RFP work:


**Product** **Who it's for** **Can you build this RFP agent?**


Microsoft Copilot (free, personal) Personal Outlook.com, Hotmail, and Live accounts Don't expect to. Custom agents with skills aren't part of the free personal plan.


Microsoft 365 Copilot Chat Work and school accounts Agent creation may be available, depending on your tenant. Grounding in work data can require a license or pay-as-you-go billing.


Microsoft 365 Copilot (licensed) Work accounts with a Copilot license Yes. This is what we used. Custom skills are a preview feature your admin may need to enable.


Copilot Studio Makers and IT teams building advanced agents Yes, with more control over connectors and publishing. Separate licensing or trial.


> **Before you start:** Custom skills in Agent Builder are a preview feature. Whether you see them depends on your organization's licensing, preview enrollment, and admin settings. If your Agent Builder doesn't show a **Skills** section, you can still build the agent and put the skill workflows into its instructions. We cover that in the troubleshooting section.


You may also come across **Copilot Cowork** , which has its own way of working with skills. Everything in this guide uses **Agent Builder** in Microsoft 365 Copilot, because that's where most proposal teams already work.


## **Pros and cons of Copilot for RFP responses**


**Pros** **Cons**


Works inside Word, Teams, and SharePoint, where your content already is Licensing is confusing, and key features are still in preview


Can ground answers in SharePoint content you control Answer quality depends entirely on how well that content is maintained


Respects your existing Microsoft 365 permissions No built-in assignment, SME review, or approval workflow for bids


Instructions and skills make results repeatable across the team You still have to test it and check its output by hand


No extra tool to buy if you already have Copilot Final formatting and portal submission are still manual


## **Before you build: set up your RFP knowledge base**


Building your[Knowledge Hub](https://www.inventive.ai/features/knowledge-hub) is the least exciting step and the one that decides whether your agent is any good. Copilot can only be as accurate as the content you point it at. If your SharePoint is full of 2022 drafts and three versions of the security policy, the agent will cite them confidently.


Spend an hour setting up a dedicated library before you open Agent Builder.


1. **Create one approved library.** Make a SharePoint site or document library just for RFP content, for example "RFP Approved Content". Don't point the agent at your whole intranet.
2. **Organize it by topic.** Folders like Company Overview, Product, Security & Compliance, Implementation, Support & SLAs, Case Studies, and Approved Q&A work well.
3. **Add metadata columns.** These make freshness checks possible later (see the table below).
4. **Archive what's obsolete.** Move superseded versions to a separate Archive library the agent can't see. One current version per topic.
5. **Lock down access.** Give most people read-only access and a small group of content owners edit rights. Copilot only shows people content they already have access to, so permissions matter.


**Column** **Why it helps**


Content owner Who to ask when an answer needs confirming


Last reviewed Lets the Content Freshness skill spot stale material


Expiry date For certifications, insurance, and attestations


Status Approved, Draft, or Archived, so only approved content is used


Content type Policy, Certification, Case Study, Q&A, and so on


> **Tip:** Put the review date inside each document too, for example in the footer. Metadata isn't always visible to the agent, but text in the document usually is.


## **What you'll build**


One agent, five skills, each covering a different stage of the response process.


**Component** **What it does**


RFP Compliance Analyst (agent) Runs the overall workflow and enforces the evidence rules


RFP Requirement Extraction Turns the solicitation into a traceable requirements matrix


Source Verification Checks draft answers against approved company sources


Compliance Coverage Finds requirements that are unanswered or only partly answered


Content Freshness Flags expired certifications, old metrics, and stale policies


Response Consistency Catches contradictions across sections and attachments


Think of the agent as the analyst and the skills as its playbooks. Extraction tells you what the buyer wants. Verification tells you what you can actually prove. Coverage shows the gaps. Freshness and consistency are your final quality pass before anything goes out the door.


## **Step 1: Open Agent Builder**


Sign in to Microsoft 365 Copilot with your work account. In the left sidebar, hover over **Agents** and choose **New agent** . You'll also see a **New agent** card on the agents page that mentions adding "custom knowledge and skills". Either one works.


*The Agents menu in Microsoft 365 Copilot, with the New agent option and the Agent Builder card.*


That opens Agent Builder. You can start from a template, but we went straight to the message box and described the agent in plain English.


*Agent Builder's starting screen. Describe your agent in the message box, or pick a template.*


> **Tip:** Can't find New agent? Your admin may have restricted agent creation. Ask before you spend time troubleshooting.


## **Step 2: Describe the agent you want**


Agent Builder generates a first draft of the agent from your description. The more specific you are, the less cleanup you'll do later. This is close to the prompt we used:


```text
Create a Microsoft Copilot agent for RFP response teams named
"RFP Compliance Analyst." Add a reusable skill named
"RFP Requirement Extraction."


The skill must:
1. Accept an uploaded RFP, RFI, RFQ, or proposal questionnaire.
2. Extract every explicit requirement, including requirements in
tables and appendices where accessible.
3. Assign each requirement a unique ID.
4. Classify requirements as mandatory, scored, informational,
contractual, or administrative.
5. Capture the exact source wording, document section, and page
number when verifiable, plus submission deadlines, word or
character limits, and the required response format.
6. Flag anything ambiguous, conflicting, or unverifiable.
7. Never invent requirements or claim the bidder complies without
supporting evidence.
```


Give it a minute. Agent Builder splits into two panels: your conversation on the left and the live configuration on the right.


*Agent Builder after the first prompt: the conversation on the left, the generated name, description, and instructions on the right.*


### **Review the name and description**


Agent Builder fills in a name and description for you. Read them carefully. The description is what colleagues see when they find your agent, so it should say plainly what the agent does and doesn't do. Ours ended up as:


```text
Helps RFP response teams turn uploaded RFPs, RFIs, RFQs, proposal questionnaires, and supporting documents into traceable requirement inventories, compliance matrices, risk flags, and action summaries. It keeps document facts separate from recommendations, marks unverifiable details for review, and avoids drafting final answers or claiming compliance without evidence.
```


### **Tighten the instructions**


The **Instructions** box is the agent's rulebook. The generated version is a good start, but we edited it to make the evidence rules explicit. Click the pencil icon to edit, or use **Suggest improvements** to have Copilot tidy it up. Here's the core of what we landed on:


```text
ROLE
You are an RFP compliance analyst supporting proposal and
bid-response teams. Help users understand solicitation
obligations, organize response work, and identify submission
risks from the documents they provide.


OPERATING GUIDELINES
- Treat the uploaded solicitation and its supporting documents
as the sole authority for document-specific claims.
- Clearly separate Extracted facts from Recommendations.
- Preserve exact source wording and traceability.
- State "Needs verification" whenever a requirement, location,
page, deadline, limit, format, or scoring weight can't be
confirmed.
- Never invent deadlines, scoring weights, requirements,
certifications, capabilities, customers, or citations.
- Use only approved company knowledge for company-specific
claims. Don't fill gaps with general knowledge.
- Never claim the bidder meets a requirement without verified
supporting evidence.
- Ask a clarifying question only when it's essential to proceed;
otherwise state your assumptions.
- Use the attached skills when available, and don't imply a
skill ran if it didn't.
```


Notice the pattern: almost every rule is about what to do when the agent **doesn't** know something. That's deliberate. In RFP work, a confident wrong answer is worse than an honest "I couldn't verify this".


> **Tip:** Keep the agent instructions about **who** the agent is and **what rules it follows** . Put detailed step-by-step procedures in skills. If you cram everything into the instructions, they get long and the agent starts skipping parts.


## **Step 3: Add the five reusable skills**


Scroll down the configuration panel to **Skills** . At first it says "Add skills to specialize this agent". Click the small arrow next to **Add** and you'll see two options:


- **Create with chat:** describe the skill and let Agent Builder write it for you.
- **Upload:** add a skill package you've already written.


*The Skills section with the Add menu open, showing Create with chat and Upload.*


We chose **Upload** because we wanted precise control over each workflow. If you're just experimenting, Create with chat is a perfectly good place to start. Want to skip writing them yourself? All five skill files are in the downloadable pack at the end of this guide.


### **How a skill package works**


A skill is a folder containing a file called **SKILL.md** . The top of the file has a short YAML header with the skill's **name** and **description** , followed by the instructions in plain Markdown. You zip the folder and upload the zip.


```text
rfp-requirement-extraction.zip
└── rfp-requirement-extraction/
└── SKILL.md
```


The start of the **SKILL.md** looks like this:


```text
---
name: rfp-requirement-extraction
description: Extract, classify, and organize every requirement in
an RFP, RFI, RFQ, or proposal questionnaire into a traceable
compliance matrix. Use when a user needs requirements, deadlines,
evaluation criteria, submission instructions, or compliance
risks identified.
---


# RFP Requirement Extraction
...
```


A few things that save headaches:


- **Keep the folder name and the name field identical.** Lowercase with hyphens is safest.
- **Write the description for the agent, not for humans.** The agent reads it to decide when to use the skill, so say exactly what it does and when.
- **Upload the zip, not the loose Markdown file.**
- **Check the limits in the upload dialog.** File size, instruction length, and skills per agent can change while the feature is in preview.


Upload the five zips one at a time. After each one, open it and check that the name, description, and instructions came through cleanly.


### **Skill 1: RFP Requirement Extraction**


This is the foundation. It reads the solicitation and turns it into a numbered, traceable list of everything the buyer is asking for.


What makes it useful is the discipline. It doesn't just pull out obvious "shall" statements. It goes through tables, appendices, footnotes, and forms, and splits compound requirements when different parts need different owners. Every requirement gets an ID like **REQ-001** , a category, an obligation status, and a source location. If it can't verify a page number, it writes **Not verified** instead of guessing.


The output starts with a quick overview (issuer, deadline, time zone, missing attachments, top risks) followed by the matrix:


**Field** **What goes in it**


Requirement ID Unique tracking ID, e.g. REQ-014


Requirement Exact wording or a clearly marked paraphrase


Category Mandatory/Pass-Fail, Scored, Technical, Security, Legal, Pricing, Administrative, and so on


Obligation Mandatory, Optional, or Not specified, never inferred


Source location File name plus verified page or section


Evidence needed What you'll need to prove it


Suggested owner A role, or Unassigned


Risk / notes Ambiguity, conflicts, disqualification risk


One rule we'd underline: the skill must not mark something mandatory just because it sounds important. If the RFP doesn't say so, the obligation is **Not specified** .


### **Skill 2: Source Verification**


A beautifully written answer can still be wrong. This skill checks drafts against your approved sources, one claim at a time.


It breaks each answer into individual factual claims, looks for evidence in your approved documents, and labels each one **Supported** , **Partially supported** , **Unsupported** , **Conflicting evidence** , or **Needs current confirmation** . Where there's no evidence, it doesn't patch the gap. It suggests a question for the right owner instead.


The output is a claim audit table. Here's an illustrative example:


**Claim ID** **Draft claim** **Evidence / source** **Status** **Recommended fix**


C-01 "We support SSO via SAML 2.0" Security Overview v4, §3.2 Supported Approve


C-02 "99.99% uptime guaranteed" No matching source Unsupported Confirm SLA with product owner


Two rules matter most here. A draft answer is never proof of itself. And generic marketing language ("enterprise-grade security") isn't evidence that a specific certification or capability exists.


### **Skill 3: Compliance Coverage**


Once you have a matrix and a draft, this skill answers the question every proposal manager asks at 11pm before a deadline: **did we answer everything?**


It maps each requirement ID to where it's answered in the draft, then rates coverage as **Addressed** , **Partially addressed** , **Not addressed** , **Evidence missing** , **Conflict** , or **Not assessable** . It won't treat a keyword match as a real answer. If the RFP asks for three things and you covered two, that's partial.


It finishes with a prioritized list: mandatory items not fully covered first, then high-value scored criteria, missing attachments, and anything that needs a clarification question to the buyer.


### **Skill 4: Content Freshness**


Reused content is the quiet killer in RFPs. That SOC 2 report you cite every time? It might have expired. The headcount in your boilerplate might be two years old.


This skill scans for time-sensitive claims (certifications, insurance, security attestations, SLAs, pricing, metrics, customer references) and classifies each as **Expired** , **Potentially stale** , **Current per supplied evidence** , **Date not established, verify** , or **Conflicting dates** .


The important nuance: a missing date isn't the same as an expired one. Both need a check, but they're different findings, and the skill keeps them separate. It also never invents a "current" value to replace an old one. This is where the review dates in your knowledge base pay off.


### **Skill 5: Response Consistency**


Big proposals are written by many people, and it shows. One section says implementation takes four weeks, the project plan says six. The executive summary promises "24/7 support", the SLA appendix says business hours.


This skill compares repeated figures, dates, names, service levels, timelines, and commitments across all sections and attachments. For every issue it shows **both** statements and **both** locations, then classifies it as **Confirmed conflict** , **Possible inconsistency, verify** , or **Terminology inconsistency** .


What it won't do is pick a winner. Deciding which number is right is a human call, usually for whoever owns that commitment.


## **Step 4: Connect your approved knowledge**


Instructions tell the agent how to behave. Knowledge tells it what's true about your company. Scroll to **Knowledge** , click **Add knowledge** , and connect the SharePoint library you set up earlier. Depending on your tenant, you can also add OneDrive files, uploaded documents, or websites.


*Skills, Knowledge, and Suggested prompts in the Agent Builder configuration panel.*


Resist the urge to connect everything. More documents don't mean better answers. Old drafts and conflicting versions make verification harder, not easier. If a file isn't something you'd happily put in front of a buyer, leave it out.


We also left **Web search** turned off. For an RFP agent, you want answers grounded in your own approved material, not whatever the internet says about your product.


> **Tip:** Keep two kinds of sources separate in your head. The solicitation tells you what the buyer requires. Your approved knowledge tells you what you can prove. Neither should stand in for the other.


## **Step 5: Set up suggested prompts**


Suggested prompts are the one-click starters people see when they open the agent. They matter more than you'd think: most people won't write a careful prompt, but they'll click a button. Scroll to **Suggested prompts** and add a title and message for each. These are the ones we set up:


**Title** **Message**


Extract Requirements Analyze this uploaded RFP and produce a complete compliance matrix with requirement IDs, categories, obligation status, verified source locations, and evidence needed. Flag ambiguities and conflicts instead of guessing.


Review Submission Risks Identify ambiguous instructions, conflicts, missing information, and potential disqualification risks in this solicitation. For each, cite the source location, explain the impact, and recommend an action.


Summarize Deadlines Extract all submission deadlines, milestones, word limits, required formats, attachments, and delivery instructions. Preserve original wording, include time zones, and flag any conflicting dates.


Map Owners and Evidence Recommend owner roles and the evidence needed for each extracted requirement. Group by function and highlight requirements with no obvious evidence source.


To improve your prompts, read our guide on[prompt engineering for RFP responses](https://www.inventive.ai/blog-posts/prompt-engineering-for-rfp-responses) .


Once the agent is saved, these show up as cards right under the message box:


*The finished RFP Compliance Analyst agent, with suggested prompts shown as cards.*


## **Step 6: Create and share**


Click **Create** in the top right of Agent Builder. Before you do, run through a quick checklist:


- Name and description clearly explain what the agent does
- Instructions spell out the evidence rules
- All five skills appear under Skills
- Knowledge points at your approved library only
- Suggested prompts cover your team's most common tasks


Hold off on sharing it widely until you've tested it (next section). Start with a small group of proposal managers, collect feedback over a couple of bids, then widen access.


## **The complete Copilot RFP workflow**


With the agent built, here's how to use it on a real bid, from the moment the RFP lands to the final sign-off. Each stage includes a prompt you can copy straight into the agent.


### **1. Extract requirements**


Upload the RFP and all its attachments, then click **Extract Requirements** or use:


```text
Extract every requirement from the attached RFP and its
appendices. Build a compliance matrix with requirement IDs,
category, obligation, verified source location, evidence needed,
and risk notes. List any referenced attachments that are missing.
```


Before going further, spot-check 10 to 15 requirements against the original document, especially the ones in tables.


### **2. Decide go or no-go**


Not every RFP is worth answering. Ask the agent to lay out the facts, then let people make the call:


```text
Using the compliance matrix and our approved knowledge, summarize
the go/no-go factors for this RFP: mandatory requirements we may
not meet, evidence gaps, unusual contract terms, deadline risk,
and effort. Separate facts from judgment. Don't make the final
recommendation; list the questions leadership should answer.
```


### **3. Understand the evaluation criteria**


Knowing how you'll be scored tells you where to spend your writing time:


```text
List the evaluation criteria and any stated weights or scoring
method, with source locations. Map each requirement ID to the
criterion it most likely affects, and mark any mapping that is
inferred rather than stated.
```


### **4. Draft responses**


Draft one section at a time, so you can review as you go:


```text
Draft answers for REQ-010 to REQ-025 using only our approved
knowledge sources. Respect each word limit. Cite the source for
every factual claim. Where no approved source exists, write
[SME INPUT NEEDED: question] instead of filling the gap.
```


Those **\[SME INPUT NEEDED\]** markers become your to-do list for subject-matter experts.


### **5. Verify claims**


Run every drafted section through source verification before it goes into the master document:


```text
Verify each factual claim in this draft against our approved
sources. Return a claim audit table and a revised answer that only
keeps supported claims.
```


### **6. Check coverage, freshness, and consistency**


When the full draft is assembled, run the three final checks:


```text
Compare the attached draft proposal against the compliance
matrix. Then check it for outdated claims and for contradictions
across sections and attachments. Give me one prioritized issue
list, with mandatory gaps first.
```


### **7. Human approval**


The agent's output is a draft, never a sign-off. Before submission, the proposal manager should confirm that every mandatory requirement is answered, each **\[SME INPUT NEEDED\]** is resolved, and anything contractual has been reviewed by legal or the accountable owner.


## **Test and measure accuracy**


This is the step people skip, and it's the one that matters most. An agent that looks polished in a demo can still miss a requirement buried in Appendix C.


Build a small **benchmark set** : two or three non-confidential past RFPs where you already know the right answers, plus a handful of deliberately tricky cases. Write down the expected result **before** you run anything.


**Test** **How to set it up** **It passes if...**


Hidden requirement An RFP with a requirement tucked inside a table or appendix It's in the matrix, with the right source location


Unsupported claim A draft answer with a claim your sources don't back up The claim is flagged Unsupported, with no made-up citation


Missing answer A draft that leaves one mandatory requirement unanswered Coverage flags it by requirement ID


Stale evidence A certificate with an expired date It's flagged Expired, and no replacement is invented


Conflicting facts Two documents with different implementation timelines Both statements and locations are shown, and neither is picked


Then track a few simple numbers each time you run the benchmark:


**Metric** **How to calculate it** **What good looks like**


Requirement recall Requirements found ÷ requirements in your answer key As close to 100% as possible, especially for mandatory items


Unsupported claim rate Unsupported claims that got through ÷ total claims Trending toward zero


Citation accuracy Citations that point to the right place ÷ citations checked High, and never invented


False alarms Issues flagged that weren't real Low enough that reviewers still trust the flags


If something keeps going wrong, fix the skill or instruction that controls it and rerun the benchmark. Test in the agent's normal chat too, not just the builder preview, because behavior can differ slightly between the two.


## **Troubleshooting**


### **There's no Skills section**


Custom skills are a preview feature that needs to be enabled for your tenant. Ask your Microsoft 365 admin. In the meantime, paste the most important skill workflows into the agent's instructions. You lose some modularity, but it still works.


### **The skill upload fails**


Check that the zip contains **SKILL.md** , that the YAML header has both **name** and **description** , that the folder name matches the **name** field, and that you're within the limits shown in the upload dialog.


### **The agent ignores a skill**


Usually the skill's description is too vague, so the agent doesn't realize it applies. Rewrite it to say exactly when to use it ("Use when a user asks whether a draft answers every requirement"). Also check that the main instructions don't contradict the skill.


### **Answers include claims you can't find in your sources**


Make sure web search is off, confirm your knowledge library is connected, and ask the agent to cite evidence for each claim. If it can't, the right output is "SME input needed", not a plausible-sounding sentence.


## **Where Copilot reaches its limits**


To be clear, this setup is genuinely useful. If your team handles a few RFPs a month and lives in Microsoft 365, it can save real hours and catch real mistakes. But as volume grows, a few problems show up:


- **Coordination.** Assigning 300 questions across 15 SMEs, chasing replies, and tracking who approved what isn't what a chat agent is built for.
- **Content upkeep.** Someone has to own the SharePoint library. If nobody does, the agent will faithfully cite outdated material.
- **Verification at scale.** Running claim audits section by section works for one bid. Across ten parallel bids, it becomes a job in itself.
- **Exports.** Getting answers into a buyer's portal, Excel questionnaire, or Word template is still manual.
- **Moving targets.** Preview features and licensing change, so your setup needs periodic rechecking.


That's the line between an AI assistant and an RFP response platform. The assistant helps you think. The platform helps you run the whole process.

## Frequently Asked Questions


### Can I build this with a free Microsoft account?


Not really. The free Copilot that comes with personal Outlook.com accounts is great for chat, but custom agents with skills and SharePoint knowledge need a Microsoft 365 work account, and usually a Copilot license or Copilot Studio.


### Is my RFP data safe in Copilot?


Microsoft 365 Copilot works within your organization's Microsoft 365 environment and permissions, so people only see content they already have access to. Still, follow your company's data policies, especially for customer RFPs under NDA, and check with IT before uploading confidential documents.


### Can Microsoft Copilot read an uploaded RFP?


Yes. Copilot can work with uploaded documents in supported formats to extract requirements, summarize instructions, and review drafts. Always check extracted requirements against the original, especially tables, scanned pages, and appendices.


### Do I need to code to build this?


No. Agent Builder is configured in plain language, and skills are Markdown files. If you can write a clear process document, you can write a skill.


### What's the difference between agent instructions and skills?


Instructions define who the agent is and the rules it always follows. Skills are task-specific playbooks the agent uses when a request matches. Keep rules in instructions and procedures in skills.


### How many skills can one agent have?


There's a cap, and it may change while the feature is in preview. Check Microsoft's current documentation or the upload dialog in your tenant. Five skills is a sensible number for one focused agent.


### Can the agent guarantee our proposal is compliant?


No, and you shouldn't want it to claim that. It can surface gaps, unsupported claims, and conflicts, but final compliance is a human decision, ideally with legal review for anything binding.


### How do I give Copilot our company’s RFP process knowledge?


Copilot won’t pick up your process by watching your team work, so you have to spell it out. The easiest approach is to split it into three parts. Rules go into the agent’s instructions: who approves what, which terms to use, what never to promise. Step-by-step workflows become skills. Reference material like your playbook and review checklists goes into the agent’s knowledge library. Then test it with real scenarios: “A security question just came in. Who needs to review it?” If the answer matches what your team actually does, you’re set.


### Can I upload a questionnaire to Copilot to check whether my response answers every question?


Yes, and it’s one of the best time-savers in the whole setup. Upload the original questionnaire alongside your draft, then ask Copilot to go question by question and mark each one Addressed, Partially addressed, or Not addressed. Ask it to put the gaps at the top so you know where to start. With the Compliance Coverage skill added, it goes a step further and catches answers that sound right but skip part of a multi-part question. It’s not a substitute for a final read-through, but it’ll find the misses you’d hate to discover after submission.

## **Wrapping up**


Using Copilot for RFPs well comes down to a few moves: clean up your knowledge base, describe the agent, tighten its rules, add your skills, and test it against answers you already know. The skills handle extraction, verification, coverage, freshness, and consistency the same way every time.


Start small. One past RFP, one approved library, and a written answer key. Fix what breaks, then roll it out to your team. And when the coordination work starts outweighing the writing, that's your signal to look at a purpose-built platform.
